analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical makers to prove their products are safe before selling them, and lets EPA restrict unsafe ones.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the Safe Chemicals Act in December 2012, but it never received a vote by the full Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled the 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act, under which thousands of chemicals on the market were never fully reviewed for safety. It would have flipped the burden of proof: instead of the EPA having to show a chemical is dangerous, manufacturers and processors would have had to show a chemical is safe before selling it. It would have created a public database of chemical safety information, narrowed the trade-secret exemptions companies could claim, kept states free to set stricter rules, and given citizens an easier path to sue over violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, workers who handle chemicals, and communities facing heavy exposures, plus state governments that keep their power to set stricter rules. Consumers get a public database of what is known about the chemicals in everyday products.

how_it_helps.text: The bill puts the burden of proof on manufacturers and processors: they must establish that a chemical meets a safety standard based only on human health and environmental considerations, with special attention to vulnerable groups like children, pregnant women, and workers.

New chemicals and new uses of existing chemicals could not be manufactured unless the EPA found they were likely to meet the safety standard, and substances of very high concern faced restrictions within 18 months.

The bill narrows the 'confidential business information' shield companies use to hide data, requires an internet-accessible public database of chemical toxicity and exposure information, and requires disclosure of chemicals found in products intended for children.
Workers and their bargaining agents would gain access to safety information on chemicals they come into contact with on the job.

States keep the right to adopt or enforce requirements stricter than federal ones, citizens can sue and petition over violations, and the cap on civil and criminal penalties is raised, including prison time for knowing violations that put people in imminent danger.

The bill closes the export loophole — companies could no longer ship banned or unreviewed chemicals abroad without accountability — and implements the Stockholm, Rotterdam, and persistent-organic-pollutants treaties.
Priority chemicals are front-loaded: 20 to 30 of the worst substances get immediate risk management, and safety determinations must begin with the most hazardous, most widely-exposed substances.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and processors, who would bear the cost of safety testing, data submission, and compliance, and who would lose the ability to keep safety data secret or export banned chemicals. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for testing and data submission would be substantial for the chemical industry, and companies argued the cost and pace of reviews could slow the introduction of new, potentially beneficial products; the bill itself acknowledges cost and feasibility considerations in setting test requirements.

The bill bars judicial review of several key agency actions — including a determination that a manufacturer failed to prove a chemical is safe — which industry critics saw as removing a basic check on regulator decisions.

The scale of work is enormous: the EPA would have to run safety determinations on batches of thousands of existing chemicals on statutory deadlines, and fee caps are repealed so industry pays the administrative cost — a design that concentrates enormous discretion in one agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real compliance cost for chemical makers against closing a decades-old gap in which thousands of chemicals were sold without any safety review — the bill's own findings note Americans carry hundreds of hazardous chemicals in their bodies and some disease rates linked to chemical exposure are rising. The bill is broadly written in the public's favor, though its bar on court review of adverse determinations and the size of the EPA workload are fair critiques that a serious compromise would have addressed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar on December 27, 2012, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced the Safe Chemicals Act of 2011 on April 14, 2011 with a list of 30 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.
The committee held hearings in November 2011 and July 2012, and on July 25, 2012 ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On December 27, 2012, Chair Barbara Boxer reported the bill to the Senate with amendments in Report 112-264, and committee Republicans filed minority views.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 578 on December 27, 2012 — two days before the 112th Congress ended — and never received a floor vote.

Under the pre-existing 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act, thousands of chemicals remained on the market without adequate safety review, and the bill's findings state that some diseases linked to chemical exposures were on the rise.
The bill had no Republican cosponsors; all 29 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers, who continued operating under the 1976 law without new testing requirements, without the burden of proving safety, and without losing their confidential-business-information and export exemptions. The public continued bearing the exposure risk the bill was written to reduce.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers, not the exposed public

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on; the bill cleared committee with minority views filed by Republicans and never reached a floor vote where the split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would impose testing, data-submission, and compliance costs, shift the burden of proving safety onto them, narrow their confidential-business-information shield, end their export exemption, and let states pile on stricter rules. Their interest in keeping the 1976 status quo ran against the public's interest in knowing chemicals are safe.

industries.industry: Downstream manufacturers that use chemicals in products
industries.note: They would face some compliance and reformulation costs, but would gain access to better public safety data and could market products as meeting a modern safety standard.

The bill creates market incentives, grants, and a network of green chemistry research centers to reward safer alternatives, which stands to benefit firms developing substitutes for hazardous chemicals.
